extracted.intended_audience: Administrators and decision-makers in the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO), South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for DIRCO officials on making and communicating administrative decisions in compliance with the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act (PAJA), ensuring decisions are lawful, reasonable, procedurally fair and that affected persons are informed of reasons and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful (authorised by law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must be allowed by law and taken by a person authorised to do so; administrators must be able to show a specific law (empowering provision) that gives them authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If decisions are not allowed by law they are unlawful and invalid. Laws often place conditions on authorisation (e.g. decision must be made by an official of a certain rank or with certain qualifications); a decision made by someone lacking required qualifications will not be authorised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable (rational and justifiable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision taken must be justifiable and there must be a good reason for it; it must be reasonable and rational—making sense given available information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rational connection must exist between a legitimate governmental purpose and the measures adopted. All relevant factors should be taken into account and the decision should be based upon findings of fact and the application of legal principles to those facts. Administrative action can be reviewed if not rationally connected to its purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedurally fair (fair procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedure must be followed that enables consultation, representation and communication of a decision and rights; affected persons must be given adequate notice and opportunity to make representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate notice means the person must know the nature and purpose of the proposed action and why it is being proposed. Persons must be given a reasonable time to make presentations, provide new information, raise objections or answer charges. Failure to follow a fair procedure allows affected persons to apply to court to have the decision reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to written reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected persons must be informed of their right to request written reasons for a decision and how to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affected persons must be informed they can request reasons within 90 days of the decision being made; information should be given on where, when and how reasons may be requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of proposed decision and opportunity to make representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to making a decision, notice should be given of the proposed decision and the affected person must be allowed to make representations regarding the proposed action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice should include what decision is being planned and why. The opportunity to make representations includes supplying new information, raising objections and answering charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empowering provision (basis in law or instrument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action must be based on an empowering provision — a law, rule of common law, customary law or agreement/instrument which purportedly authorises the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of empowering provisions include the Public Service Act, Public Service Regulations and DIRCO policies. Decisions must be made under such a provision to be lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of administrative action (six elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action consists of elements including: a decision of an administrative nature, an empowering provision, fair procedure, lawfulness, organ of state, and reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions taken as part of daily tasks are usually administrative and must satisfy these elements to fall under PAJA. Excluded are policy decisions of the executive, legislative acts, and judicial functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal effect (component of administrative action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must be legally binding (have legal effect) to constitute administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only decisions with legal force qualify; purely beneficial decisions may not constitute administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct effect (component of administrative action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must be final and directly affect the person (if multiple steps are involved, only the final step that affects a member of the public counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a decision requires several steps, only the last step that effects the person will constitute administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: External effect (component of administrative action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must affect someone who is not part of DIRCO (an external person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effect is internal to DIRCO, it may not be 'administrative action' under PAJA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication of decision in plain language
rubrics_metrics.description: The affected person must be informed of the decision in writing using plain and straightforward language that is easy to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication should also inform the person of their right to request reasons and of available review or appeal routes, including where/when/how and time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information about internal appeal or review procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: If an internal appeal procedure exists, the affected person must be informed how and where to appeal and what time limits apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no internal appeal exists, the affected person must be informed they may approach a court to ask for the decision to be reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: time limits and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected persons may challenge administrative decisions in court (judicial review) within 180 days (6 months) of the final decision or the internal appeal being decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the court finds a decision unlawful, unreasonable or procedurally unfair it can declare the decision invalid, order reconsideration, substitute its own decision, or order the government to pay damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper exercise of discretionary powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretionary powers must be exercised only by the person given those powers, within the law, and for the purposes for which they are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using discretion, administrators may only take relevant factors into account; failure to consider relevant factors or taking irrelevant factors renders the decision lacking good reason and susceptible to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and absence of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators must make decisions without bias; bias means lack of independence or impartiality or being unfairly slanted in favour of a particular person or outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bias undermines procedural fairness and can be grounds for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of mistakes or non-compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action may be reviewed or set aside where it contravenes a law, is not authorised by the empowering provision, is not rationally connected to its purpose, is based on a mistake about legal requirements, or fails to follow required procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may set aside actions taken based on errors about what the law requires or where prescribed procedures or conditions were not complied with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope exclusions (what PAJA does not cover)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain decisions are excluded from PAJA, including policy decisions of the executive, the making of legislation by Parliament/provincial legislatures/municipal councils, and the exercise of judicial functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusions clarify what types of acts are not ‘administrative action’ under PAJA.
